- **55-inch commercial display:** 150-250 watts ($150-$250/year)
- **75-inch commercial display:** 250-400 watts ($250-$400/year)
- **Video wall (4x 55-inch):** 600-1,000 watts ($600-$1,000/year)
- **LED direct-view display (per sq meter):** 200-600 watts ($200-$600/year)

### Media Players
- **Basic media player:** 10-30 watts ($10-$30/year)
- **High-performance media player:** 30-65 watts ($30-$65/year)

### Audio Infrastructure
- **Networked audio player:** 5-15 watts ($5-$15/year) — negligible compared to screens
- **Amplifiers:** 50-200 watts (typically existing infrastructure)

## Reducing Energy Impact

### Automated Brightness Control
Ambient light sensors that adjust screen brightness based on natural light can reduce energy consumption by 20-40%. Screens don't need full brightness in a dimly lit store at night.

### Scheduling and Power Management
Turn screens off or to standby during non-operating hours. Some CMS platforms support automatic power scheduling. This alone can reduce energy use by 30-40%.

### Energy-Efficient Hardware
Newer commercial displays use LED backlighting and efficient processors that consume 30-50% less energy than older models. The ROI on upgrading old screens often pays for itself in 2-3 years through energy savings.

### E-Paper and Low-Power Alternatives
Electronic shelf labels and e-paper displays consume near-zero energy except during content updates. These are ideal for pricing and basic product information, reserving high-energy LCD/LED screens for high-impact advertising locations.

## Sustainability Reporting

Retailers with ESG commitments should track and report the energy consumption of their retail media infrastructure. Some retailers offset screen energy consumption with renewable energy credits or include digital signage in their broader carbon reduction targets.

title: Technology requirements to launch a retail media network
meta_title: Technology Requirements To Launch A Retail Media Networ | InStoreIndex
meta_description: Launching a retail media network requires four core technology components: a media delivery system (audio players and/or digital screens), an ad server or
h1: What Technology Do You Need to Launch a Retail Media Network?
intro: Launching a retail media network requires four core technology components: a media delivery system (audio players and/or digital screens), an ad server or content management platform, a measurement and attribution layer connected to POS data, and an advertiser-facing booking and reporting portal. Retailers can build this stack internally, license it from providers like QSIC, Stingray, or Vibenomics, or use a combination approach. Most mid-size retailers partner with a technology provider rather than building from scratch.
body_content:
## Core Technology Stack

### 1. Media Delivery Infrastructure
The physical hardware that plays ads in stores. For audio: networked media players connected to the store's speaker system. For visual: commercial-grade digital screens with media players. Cloud-managed devices allow remote content updates and scheduling.

### 2. Ad Server / Campaign Management
Software that manages ad scheduling, targeting, frequency capping, and delivery. This is the brain of the retail media network — it decides which ads play in which stores at which times. Options range from white-label platforms from providers like QSIC and Broadsign to custom-built solutions.

### 3. Measurement and Attribution
The system that connects ad exposure to purchase behavior. Requires integration with POS systems, loyalty programs, or both. Closed-loop attribution (tying an ad impression to a sale of the advertised product) is the key differentiator of retail media vs. traditional advertising.

### 4. Advertiser Portal
A self-serve or managed-service interface where advertisers can book campaigns, upload creative, set targeting, and view reporting. Self-serve portals are essential for scaling beyond a handful of managed advertisers.

## Supporting Technology

### Data Management Platform (DMP)
Aggregates and organizes shopper data from loyalty programs, POS, and other sources to enable audience targeting and measurement.

### Programmatic Integration
SSP (supply-side platform) connections that allow in-store inventory to be purchased through programmatic DSPs. This opens inventory to a much larger pool of advertisers.

### Content Moderation
Automated or manual review systems to ensure ad creative meets brand safety guidelines and retailer content policies.

## Build vs. Buy

Building a full retail media technology stack internally costs $2-10M+ and takes 12-18 months. Partnering with an established provider can get a network live in 60-90 days with minimal upfront capital. Most retailers start with a partner and gradually bring capabilities in-house as revenue grows.

title: Retail media network revenue share models explained
meta_title: Retail Media Network Revenue Share Models Explained | InStoreIndex
meta_description: Retail media network revenue share models typically split advertising revenue between the retailer and the technology or media sales partner. Standard spli
h1: Retail Media Network Revenue Share Models: How Retailers and Tech Partners Split Revenue
intro: Retail media network revenue share models typically split advertising revenue between the retailer and the technology or media sales partner. Standard splits range from 50/50 to 80/20 in favor of the retailer, depending on who owns the advertiser relationship, the technology platform, and the sales effort. In-store audio networks commonly offer retailers 40-60% of ad revenue, while retailers with their own sales teams and technology may keep 80-90% of revenue minus platform fees.
body_content:
## Common Revenue Share Structures

### Technology-Led Model (40/60 to 50/50)
The technology partner (like QSIC or Vibenomics) provides the platform, sells the ad inventory, and handles campaign execution. The retailer provides the store locations and audience. Typical split: 40-50% to retailer, 50-60% to tech partner. Best for retailers without in-store media sales expertise.

### Retailer-Led Model (70/30 to 85/15)
The retailer has a dedicated retail media team that sells directly to brands. The technology partner provides the platform and takes a smaller revenue share or flat platform fee. Typical split: 70-85% to retailer, 15-30% to tech partner. Common among large retailers like Walmart and Kroger.

### Hybrid Model (55/45 to 65/35)
A mix where the tech partner handles some sales (programmatic and aggregated demand) while the retailer sells premium sponsorships directly. Revenue splits differ by sales channel. Increasingly popular as retailers build internal capabilities.

### SaaS Model (Retailer Keeps 100% Minus Fees)
The retailer pays a monthly SaaS fee for the technology platform and keeps 100% of advertising revenue. More common with digital signage CMS platforms than audio advertising networks.

## Factors That Affect Revenue Share

Several variables shift the negotiation: store count and traffic (more stores = more leverage), exclusivity terms, contract length, who provides hardware, who manages advertiser relationships, and whether the retailer provides first-party data for targeting. Retailers with strong loyalty programs and rich shopper data can command better splits.

## Revenue Expectations

In-store audio advertising typically generates $100-$500 per store per month at the network level. Digital screen networks can generate $500-$3,000+ per store per month depending on screen count and traffic. These figures vary widely based on store traffic, advertiser demand, and market maturity.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Arkansas (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Arkansas (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Arkansas. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Arkansas
intro: Playing music in your business in Arkansas? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Arkansas. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Arkansas may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Arkansas need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Arkansas

All businesses in Arkansas that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Arkansas

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Arkansas

Businesses in Arkansas caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Arkansas.

## Arkansas Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Arkansas, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in Arkansas?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Arkansas playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Arkansas?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Arkansas business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in New Mexico (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in New Mexico (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in New Mexico. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in New Mexico
intro: Playing music in your business in New Mexico? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in New Mexico. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and New Mexico may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in New Mexico need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in New Mexico

All businesses in New Mexico that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in New Mexico

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in New Mexico

Businesses in New Mexico caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across New Mexico.

## New Mexico Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in New Mexico, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in New Mexico?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in New Mexico playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in New Mexico?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my New Mexico business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Montana (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Montana (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Montana. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Montana
intro: Playing music in your business in Montana? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Montana. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Montana may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Montana need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Montana

All businesses in Montana that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Montana

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Montana

Businesses in Montana caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Montana.

## Montana Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Montana, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in Montana?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Montana playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Montana?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Montana business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Tennessee
intro: Playing music in your business in Tennessee? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Tennessee. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Tennessee may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Tennessee need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Tennessee

All businesses in Tennessee that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Tennessee

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Tennessee

Businesses in Tennessee caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Tennessee.

## Tennessee Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Tennessee, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

title: Brand safety guidelines for in-store retail media
meta_title: Brand Safety Guidelines For In-Store Retail Media | InStoreIndex
meta_description: Brand safety in in-store retail media means ensuring that ad content played in stores is appropriate for the environment, compliant with regulations, and a
h1: Brand Safety in In-Store Retail Media: Guidelines for Retailers and Advertisers
intro: Brand safety in in-store retail media means ensuring that ad content played in stores is appropriate for the environment, compliant with regulations, and aligned with both the retailer's values and the advertiser's brand guidelines. Unlike digital advertising where brand safety concerns center on ad adjacency to harmful content, in-store brand safety focuses on content appropriateness for a public physical space — including volume levels, message tone, competitive conflicts, and category restrictions.
body_content:
## Retailer Brand Safety Considerations

### Content Approval Process
Every ad creative should go through a review process before going live. Retailers should maintain clear content guidelines covering language, imagery, claims, and category restrictions. Most retail media networks build an approval workflow into their ad server.

### Category Restrictions
Common restricted categories include alcohol, tobacco, firearms, political advertising, and competitor products. Grocery retailers may restrict ads from brands not carried in their stores. Pharmacies restrict pharmaceutical advertising to comply with FDA regulations.

### Volume and Tone
Audio ads that are significantly louder than the background music or use jarring sound effects create a negative experience. Ads should match the ambient energy of the store and time of day.

### Competitive Separation
Avoid playing ads from direct competitors back-to-back. Maintain minimum separation rules (typically 15-30 minutes) between ads in the same product category.

## Advertiser Brand Safety Considerations

### Environment Alignment
Brands should verify that the retail environment aligns with their brand values. A luxury brand may not want ads playing in a discount retailer, and vice versa.

### Adjacent Content
What plays before and after the ad matters. A health food brand doesn't want to follow a fast food ad. Networks should offer category adjacency controls.

### Audience Verification
Advertisers should confirm that the store's shopper demographics match their target audience. Request foot traffic data and shopper profiles before committing to campaigns.

## Industry Standards

The IAB (Interactive Advertising Bureau) has published guidelines for retail media that include brand safety recommendations. The In-Store Media Association is also developing standards for physical retail environments. As the industry matures, expect more formalized brand safety certification programs.

title: Retail media attribution windows explained
meta_title: Retail Media Attribution Windows Explained | InStoreIndex
meta_description: An attribution window in retail media is the time period after ad exposure during which a purchase is credited to the campaign. For in-store media, common
h1: Understanding Attribution Windows in Retail Media: How Long After an Ad Should Sales Count?
intro: An attribution window in retail media is the time period after ad exposure during which a purchase is credited to the campaign. For in-store media, common attribution windows range from same-visit (the shopper purchases during the same trip they were exposed to the ad) to 7-14 days post-exposure for loyalty-tracked shoppers. The choice of attribution window significantly affects reported campaign performance — longer windows capture more conversions but include more purchases that may have happened regardless of the ad.
body_content:
## Common Attribution Windows

### Same-Visit Attribution
Credits a sale only if the shopper purchases the advertised product during the same store visit where they were exposed to the ad. This is the most conservative and credible window. Best for impulse categories and in-store audio ads.

### 24-Hour Window
Credits purchases made within 24 hours of ad exposure, including a return trip to the same store. Captures shoppers who were influenced but didn't buy immediately. Requires loyalty data to track the same shopper across visits.

### 7-Day Window
The most common window for retail media reporting. Captures delayed purchases and stock-up behavior. Industry standard for many retail media networks including Walmart Connect.

### 14-Day Window
Used for higher-consideration categories or new product launches where trial may take longer. Less common and viewed with more skepticism by sophisticated advertisers.

### Custom Windows
Some networks allow advertisers to select their preferred attribution window. This creates comparability challenges when benchmarking across networks.

## Why Attribution Windows Matter

A 7-day window will always show higher sales lift than a same-visit window because it captures more purchases. This makes it crucial to compare campaigns using the same attribution window. An advertiser seeing "15% lift" on one network (7-day window) vs. "5% lift" on another (same-visit) isn't necessarily seeing worse performance on the second network.

## Industry Best Practice

The IAB recommends that retail media networks report on multiple attribution windows so advertisers can evaluate performance at different levels of conservatism. At minimum, networks should report same-visit and 7-day results. Transparency about attribution methodology is becoming a key differentiator for retail media networks competing for advertiser dollars.

The choice of attribution window significantly affects reported campaign performance — longer windows capture more conversions but include more purchases that may have happened regardless of the ad.

- Any business playing music publicly needs performance rights licenses
- The three major PROs in the US are ASCAP, BMI, and SESAC (plus GMR)

- Penalties for unlicensed music can reach $30,000 per song

title: How to produce effective in-store audio ads
meta_title: How To Produce Effective In-Store Audio Ads | InStoreIndex
meta_description: Producing effective in-store audio ads requires a different approach than radio or podcast advertising. In-store audio plays in a noisy, distracted environ
h1: In-Store Audio Ad Production: A Guide to Creating Effective Spots
intro: Producing effective in-store audio ads requires a different approach than radio or podcast advertising. In-store audio plays in a noisy, distracted environment where shoppers are focused on their shopping mission, not actively listening. The best in-store audio ads are 15-30 seconds long, lead with a clear product benefit or offer, use conversational tone at a moderate pace, and include a simple call-to-action directing shoppers to a specific aisle or display. Professional voice talent and quality production are essential — amateur-sounding ads undermine both the brand and the retail environment.
body_content:
## In-Store Audio Ad Best Practices

### Length
- **15 seconds:** Best for simple awareness messages and promotional offers
- **30 seconds:** Best for new product introductions and more complex messages
- **60 seconds:** Generally too long for in-store; shoppers tune out after 30 seconds

### Structure (30-Second Spot)
1. **Hook (0-5 seconds):** Grab attention with a relevant need-state or question
2. **Product/Brand (5-15 seconds):** Introduce the product and key benefit
3. **Offer (15-22 seconds):** State the promotional offer if applicable
4. **Call-to-Action (22-30 seconds):** Direct shoppers where to find the product

### Voice and Tone
- Conversational, not announcer-style
- Match the energy of the store environment
- Moderate pace — slightly slower than radio to cut through ambient noise
- Avoid shouting or aggressive sales language

### Audio Production
- Record in a professional studio or use high-quality remote recording
- Mix audio levels to match the store's background music volume
- Avoid heavy music beds that compete with the store's background music
- Test playback through commercial-grade speakers, not studio monitors

## Common Mistakes

### Too Many Messages
Trying to cram multiple products or offers into one spot. One product, one message, one CTA.

### Wrong Tone for Environment
Using aggressive radio-style delivery in a calm retail environment. Match the store's vibe.

### No Clear CTA
Raising awareness without telling shoppers what to do. "Find it in aisle 7" or "Look for the display near checkout" drives action.

### Poor Audio Quality
Low-quality recording, bad microphone technique, or unbalanced levels. This reflects poorly on both the brand and the retailer.

## AI-Generated Audio Ads

Providers like QSIC now offer AI-generated audio ad creative through tools like Lucy, which can produce multiple ad variations quickly and cost-effectively. AI-generated spots are improving rapidly but still benefit from human review and editing for tone and brand alignment.

h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in North Carolina
intro: Playing music in your business in North Carolina? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in North Carolina. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and North Carolina may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in North Carolina need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in North Carolina

All businesses in North Carolina that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in North Carolina

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in North Carolina

Businesses in North Carolina caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across North Carolina.

## North Carolina Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in North Carolina, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in North Carolina playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in North Carolina?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my North Carolina business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Maryland (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Maryland (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Maryland. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Maryland
intro: Playing music in your business in Maryland? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Maryland. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Maryland may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Maryland need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Maryland

All businesses in Maryland that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Maryland

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Maryland

Businesses in Maryland caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Maryland.

## Maryland Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Maryland, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in Maryland?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Maryland playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Maryland?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Maryland business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

body_content:
## Getting Started with Minimal Investment

### Aggregated Audio Networks
The lowest-barrier entry point. Partners like QSIC, Stingray, and Vibenomics install networked media players in your stores, manage background music programming, and insert audio ads from their advertiser base. You receive a monthly revenue share check. Setup typically requires only internet connectivity and speaker system access.

### Co-Op Advertising Programs
Many CPG brands have co-op advertising budgets earmarked for retail partners. Small retailers can access these funds by offering in-store screen or audio ad placements as part of vendor marketing programs. This doesn't require a formal retail media network — just the ability to play vendor-provided content.

### Supplier-Funded Screens
Digital screen manufacturers and CMS providers sometimes offer hardware at reduced cost in exchange for ad inventory rights. The supplier fills some ad slots with their network's advertisers while the retailer uses remaining inventory for their own promotions.

## Revenue Expectations by Store Count

### 20-50 Stores
- Audio advertising: $100-$200/store/month ($2,000-$10,000/month total)
- Best approach: Join an aggregated network
- Timeline to revenue: 60-90 days

### 50-200 Stores
- Audio advertising: $200-$400/store/month ($10,000-$80,000/month total)
- Screen advertising: Additional $100-$300/store/month with screen investment
- Best approach: Aggregated network + direct sales for premium sponsorships
- Timeline to revenue: 90-120 days

### 200-500 Stores
- Combined media: $400-$800/store/month ($80,000-$400,000/month total)
- Best approach: Hybrid model with network partner + internal sales team
- Timeline to revenue: 120-180 days

## Key Success Factors

High store traffic is more important than store count. A 50-store chain with 5,000+ daily visitors per store is more attractive to advertisers than a 200-store chain with 500 visitors per store. Clean audio infrastructure, reliable internet, and willingness to share foot traffic data all increase revenue potential.

title: How incrementality testing works for retail media
meta_title: How Incrementality Testing Works For Retail Media | InStoreIndex
meta_description: Incrementality testing in retail media measures whether an advertising campaign actually caused additional sales, or whether those sales would have happene
h1: Incrementality Testing for Retail Media: Measuring True Campaign Impact
intro: Incrementality testing in retail media measures whether an advertising campaign actually caused additional sales, or whether those sales would have happened anyway. The standard approach uses test-and-control store groups: ads run in a set of test stores while matched control stores receive no ads, and the sales difference between groups reveals the true incremental lift. This is considered the gold standard for retail media measurement because it isolates the ad's impact from baseline purchasing behavior, promotions, and seasonality.
body_content:
## How Test-and-Control Works

### Store Matching
The first step is creating matched pairs of stores with similar characteristics: sales volume, shopper demographics, geography, and store format. Statistical methods like propensity score matching ensure the test and control groups are comparable.

### Campaign Execution
The advertising campaign runs only in test stores. Control stores continue with normal programming (music only, no ads, or a public service message placeholder). Both groups maintain identical pricing, promotions, and merchandising.

### Measurement Period
The test typically runs for 4-8 weeks to accumulate statistically significant data. Shorter tests risk noise; longer tests risk external variables contaminating results.

### Lift Calculation
Incremental lift = (Test store sales - Control store sales) / Control store sales. A 5% lift means the ad campaign generated 5% more sales of the advertised product compared to stores without the campaign.

## Challenges with Incrementality Testing

### Sample Size
You need enough stores in each group to reach statistical significance. Retailers with under 100 locations may struggle to create large enough test/control groups.

### Contamination
Shoppers who visit both test and control stores can blur results. Geographic separation between groups helps minimize this.

### Opportunity Cost
Control stores forgo ad revenue during the test period, which can be a hard sell internally.

## Alternatives to Test-and-Control

When full test-and-control isn't feasible, retailers use pre/post analysis (comparing sales before and after campaign launch), matched market analysis, or synthetic control methods using statistical modeling. These are less rigorous but more practical for smaller networks.

faq_questions.question: Incrementality Testing for Retail Media: Measuring True Campaign Impact
faq_questions.answer: Incrementality testing in retail media measures whether an advertising campaign actually caused additional sales, or whether those sales would have happened anyway. The standard approach uses test-and-control store groups: ads run in a set of test stores while matched control stores receive no ads, and the sales difference between groups reveals the true incremental lift. This is considered the gold standard for retail media measurement because it isolates the ad's impact from baseline purchasing behavior, promotions, and seasonality.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Kansas (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Kansas (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Kansas. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Kansas
intro: Playing music in your business in Kansas? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Kansas. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Kansas may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Kansas need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Kansas

All businesses in Kansas that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Kansas

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Kansas

Businesses in Kansas caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Kansas.

## Kansas Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Kansas, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Kansas playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Kansas?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Kansas business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

## Why Hotels Need Specialized In-Store Audio Advertising

Hotels operate in unique environments where the wrong in-store audio advertising can hurt more than help. The right solution accounts for your customer demographics, peak hours, noise levels, and brand identity.

## Top In-Store Audio Advertising Providers for Hotels

### 1. Rockbot
Rockbot is a streaming media platform for businesses offering licensed background music, digital signage, TV programming, audio messaging, and retail media advertising through one unified platform. Founded in 2009 and backed by Google, Rockbot serves nearly 50,000 businesses across North America.
- **Key Strength:** Single-platform solution for music, TV, signage, and advertising. Backed by Google. Interactive Rockbot Request feature lets guests request songs.
- **Music Library:** 18M+ songs

### 2. Stingray
Stingray is a Canadian public company (TSX: RAY.A/RAY.B) providing commercial music, digital signage, in-store audio advertising, and AI-driven consumer insights. Stingray Advertising is North America's largest retail audio advertising network, reaching 928M+ shopping visits monthly across 25,100+ locations.
- **Key Strength:** North America's largest retail audio advertising network with 25,100+ locations and 928M+ monthly shopping visits. Publicly traded with ~1,000 employees globally.

### 3. MTI
MTI is an in-store media provider offering background music, overhead messaging, and digital signage solutions for businesses. The company focuses on helping brands create consistent audio experiences across multiple locations with curated music programming and targeted messaging.
- **Key Strength:** Personalized service with direct account management and custom music programming for multi-location businesses

### 4. Mood Media
Mood Media is the world's leading in-store media provider, offering background music, digital signage, scent marketing, AV systems, and overhead messaging. Formerly Muzak, the company serves over 100,000 businesses globally with a comprehensive suite of customer experience solutions.
- **Key Strength:** Largest global in-store media provider with 88+ years of industry heritage (Muzak legacy) and 100+ expert music designers worldwide
- **Music Library:** 120M+ tracks

### 5. Soundtrack Your Brand
Soundtrack Your Brand is a Spotify-backed commercial music streaming platform that provides fully licensed background music for businesses. Known for strong UX and the largest commercially licensed music catalog, it offers on-demand track selection, custom playlist building, and multi-location management.
- **Key Strength:** Spotify-backed with the largest commercially licensed catalog. Only major platform offering true on-demand song selection and Spotify playlist import.
- **Music Library:** 58M+ songs

### 6. QSIC
QSIC is an AI-powered in-store audio platform that helps retailers monetize and measure in-store audio as a retail media channel. Founded in Australia in 2012, QSIC powers 7-Eleven's Gulp Radio across 12,000+ stores and reaches 100M+ shoppers monthly. Raised $25M Series B in January 2025 led by Hedosophia.
- **Key Strength:** AI-powered audio platform with patented ambient noise technology, closed-loop sales attribution, and AI-generated ad creative (Lucy). Powers 7-Eleven Gulp Radio across 12,000+ stores.

## What to Look For

- Content filtering and appropriateness for hotels
- Multi-location management dashboard
- Commercial music licensing included
- Hardware compatibility with existing systems
- Reliable uptime and support
- Scalable pricing as you grow

## Pricing for Hotels

Budget: $15-25/mo per location. Mid-range: $25-75/mo. Enterprise: custom pricing. Factor in hardware, installation, and any required AV equipment.

title: How AI enables personalized in-store retail media
meta_title: How Ai Enables Personalized In-Store Retail Media | InStoreIndex
meta_description: AI is enabling a shift from mass in-store advertising to personalized retail media experiences. While traditional in-store audio and signage blast the same
h1: AI-Powered Personalization in Retail Media Networks
intro: AI is enabling a shift from mass in-store advertising to personalized retail media experiences. While traditional in-store audio and signage blast the same message to every shopper, AI-powered systems can now adjust ad content based on real-time store conditions, time of day, shopper demographics, and even individual purchase history at checkout. QSIC uses AI to optimize audio ad scheduling based on store traffic and ambient noise. Smart cart and checkout screen providers use loyalty data to show personalized offers. This personalization drives higher engagement and better campaign results for advertisers.
body_content:
## How AI Personalization Works In-Store

### Real-Time Ad Scheduling
AI algorithms analyze store traffic patterns, time of day, weather, and local events to schedule the most relevant ads at optimal times. A beverage ad plays during peak afternoon traffic when thirst-driven purchases spike. A comfort food ad plays during cold weather.

### Audience-Aware Content
Systems using foot traffic sensors or Wi-Fi analytics can estimate store demographics in real time and adjust content accordingly. A store with predominantly young adult traffic mid-evening gets different ad programming than a weekend morning crowd of families.

### Checkout Personalization
Self-checkout and smart cart screens can display personalized offers based on items being scanned. A shopper buying pasta sees a sauce promotion. A shopper buying diapers sees a baby wipes offer. This requires real-time POS integration and AI recommendation engines.

### AI Audio Ad Creative
QSIC's Lucy platform generates AI audio ad creative that can be customized for different store formats, dayparts, and audience segments without requiring separate production for each variation.

## Current Limitations

True one-to-one personalization is limited in-store because overhead audio reaches everyone and most screens are one-to-many. Personalization is currently more about optimizing what plays when (contextual personalization) than personalizing for individual shoppers (except at checkout and smart cart touchpoints).

## Privacy Considerations

In-store personalization must navigate privacy regulations and shopper expectations. Anonymous, aggregate-level personalization (adjusting content based on overall traffic patterns) faces fewer concerns than individual-level targeting. Retailers should be transparent about data collection and give shoppers opt-out options through loyalty program preferences.

## Impact on Advertiser Results

Early evidence suggests AI-optimized in-store media scheduling improves sales lift by 20-40% compared to static scheduling. As personalization capabilities mature, the gap between optimized and non-optimized networks will widen, creating a competitive moat for technology-forward retail media networks.

title: How to staff and structure a retail media network team
meta_title: How To Staff And Structure A Retail Media Network Team | InStoreIndex
meta_description: A retail media network team requires a blend of advertising sales, ad operations, data analytics, and technology skills. Smaller retailers (under 500 store
h1: Retail Media Network Team Structure: Roles, Skills, and Organizational Design
intro: A retail media network team requires a blend of advertising sales, ad operations, data analytics, and technology skills. Smaller retailers (under 500 stores) typically start with 2-5 people focused on partner management and reporting, relying on technology partners for platform operations. Larger retailers build dedicated teams of 20-50+ spanning sales, operations, analytics, product, and engineering. The organizational placement of the retail media team — within marketing, merchandising, or as an independent P&L — significantly impacts its success and growth trajectory.
body_content:
## Core Roles

### Sales and Business Development
Account executives who sell ad inventory to brands and agencies. Experienced retail media sellers typically come from digital advertising, trade marketing, or media sales backgrounds. This is the revenue engine of the network.

### Ad Operations
Manages campaign setup, trafficking, scheduling, QA, and delivery monitoring. Ensures ads play correctly in the right stores at the right times. Often the first hire after sales because campaign execution can't fail.

### Data and Analytics
Builds measurement frameworks, runs attribution analyses, creates advertiser reports, and identifies optimization opportunities. Requires strong SQL, statistical analysis, and data visualization skills.

### Product and Technology
Manages the advertising platform roadmap, integrations with DSPs and SSPs, and development of advertiser-facing tools. Can be internal or managed through a technology partner.

### Content and Creative Services
Produces or reviews ad creative, manages content guidelines, and may offer creative production services to advertisers as an upsell.

## Team Size by Stage

### Startup Phase (0-12 months): 3-5 people
- 1 GM/Head of Retail Media
- 1-2 Sales leads
- 1 Ad Operations
- 1 Analytics (can be shared with broader org)

### Growth Phase (1-3 years): 10-20 people
- Sales team expands to cover categories and agencies
- Dedicated analytics and measurement team
- Product manager for platform development
- Creative services capability

### Mature Phase (3+ years): 20-50+ people
- Full category sales teams mirroring advertiser org structures
- Self-serve platform team
- Data science and advanced analytics
- Programmatic partnerships team

## Organizational Placement

The retail media team works best as an independent business unit with its own P&L, reporting to the CEO or COO. Embedding it within marketing or merchandising creates conflicts of interest and limits growth. Independent P&L status attracts better talent and enables faster decision-making.

h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Georgia
intro: Playing music in your business in Georgia? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Georgia. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Georgia may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Georgia need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Georgia

All businesses in Georgia that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Georgia

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Georgia

Businesses in Georgia caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Georgia.

## Georgia Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Georgia, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Georgia playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Georgia?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Georgia business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in South Dakota (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in South Dakota (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in South Dakota. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in South Dakota
intro: Playing music in your business in South Dakota? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in South Dakota. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and South Dakota may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in South Dakota need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in South Dakota

All businesses in South Dakota that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in South Dakota

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in South Dakota

Businesses in South Dakota caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across South Dakota.

## South Dakota Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in South Dakota, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in South Dakota?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in South Dakota playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in South Dakota?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my South Dakota business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

meta_title: Retail Media Network International Expansion Considerat | InStoreIndex

h1: Taking Your Retail Media Network International: Key Considerations
intro: Expanding a retail media network internationally introduces challenges around data privacy regulations (GDPR in Europe, LGPD in Brazil, PIPL in China), local advertising standards, content localization, technology infrastructure differences, and varying levels of advertiser demand. Successful international expansion requires partnering with local technology providers who understand regional requirements, adapting measurement methodologies to local data regulations, and building sales teams with regional market knowledge. The U.S. leads in retail media maturity, but Europe, Latin America, and Asia-Pacific are growing rapidly.
body_content:
## Key Considerations by Region

### Europe
- **GDPR compliance** is the dominant concern. Consent requirements for tracking, data minimization principles, and cross-border data transfer restrictions all affect targeting and measurement capabilities.
- **Market maturity** varies: UK and France are relatively advanced; Germany, Spain, and Italy are earlier stage.
- **Privacy-first measurement** approaches using aggregated data and clean rooms are becoming the norm.

### Latin America
- **Brazil's LGPD** mirrors GDPR with local nuances. Mexico's data protection law is less restrictive but evolving.
- **Mobile-first shoppers** create opportunities for app-based retail media alongside in-store.
- **Infrastructure challenges** including unreliable internet in some locations affect cloud-based platforms.

### Asia-Pacific
- **China's PIPL** is among the world's strictest data laws, requiring domestic data storage and explicit consent.
- **Super-app integration** (WeChat, Alipay) blurs the line between online and in-store retail media.
- **Japan and Australia** have well-developed retail markets with growing retail media programs.

## Operational Challenges

### Content Localization
Audio ads must be produced in local languages with culturally appropriate messaging. This multiplies creative production costs and requires local talent and review processes.

### Technology Infrastructure
Internet reliability, power consistency, and available hardware vary significantly by market. Some regions require local hosting and data residency.

### Advertiser Demand
The pool of advertisers buying in-store retail media is smaller outside the U.S. International expansion should be anchored by global CPG brands (Procter & Gamble, Unilever, Nestlé) that have budgets allocated across markets.

### Measurement Standards
Attribution and measurement expectations differ by market. European advertisers may accept privacy-compliant aggregate measurement that U.S. advertisers would consider insufficient.

## Recommended Approach

Start with one or two markets where you have existing retail operations and advertiser relationships. Partner with local technology providers for compliance and cultural expertise. Establish a regional P&L rather than managing international markets from a centralized team. And accept that margin and measurement will be different in early international markets compared to the mature U.S. market.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Louisiana (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Louisiana (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Louisiana. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Louisiana
intro: Playing music in your business in Louisiana? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Louisiana. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Louisiana may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Louisiana need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Louisiana

All businesses in Louisiana that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Louisiana

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Louisiana

Businesses in Louisiana caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Louisiana.

## Louisiana Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Louisiana, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in Louisiana?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Louisiana playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Louisiana?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Louisiana business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Hawaii (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Hawaii. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Hawaii
intro: Playing music in your business in Hawaii? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Hawaii. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Hawaii may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Hawaii need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Hawaii

All businesses in Hawaii that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Hawaii

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Hawaii

Businesses in Hawaii caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Hawaii.

## Hawaii Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Hawaii, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

faq_questions.question: Do I need a music license for my business in Hawaii?
faq_questions.answer: Yes. All businesses in Hawaii playing music publicly need licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, and GMR — or a commercial music service that includes these.

faq_questions.question: How much does a music license cost in Hawaii?
faq_questions.answer: Individual PRO licenses range from a few hundred to several thousand dollars per year depending on business type and size. Commercial music services start at ~$15-25/month and include all licenses.

faq_questions.question: Can I play the radio in my Hawaii business?
faq_questions.answer: Playing radio may be covered under the 'homestyle exemption' if your business is under 2,000 sq ft (retail) or 3,750 sq ft (food/drinking) and uses a limited number of speakers. Larger businesses need separate licenses.

h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Nebraska
intro: Playing music in your business in Nebraska? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Nebraska. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Nebraska may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Nebraska need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Nebraska

All businesses in Nebraska that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Nebraska

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Nebraska

Businesses in Nebraska caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Nebraska.

## Nebraska Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Nebraska, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

h1: Best Sound System Providers for Retail Stores
intro: The best sound system for retail stores combines properly licensed content, easy scheduling, and reliable multi-location management at a price that makes sense. Retail Stores have unique requirements — from content appropriateness to volume control — that generic solutions often miss. Here are the top sound system providers for retail stores in 2026, with features, pricing, and recommendations.
body_content:
## Why Retail Stores Need Specialized Sound System

Retail Stores operate in unique environments where the wrong sound system can hurt more than help. The right solution accounts for your customer demographics, peak hours, noise levels, and brand identity.

## Top Sound System Providers for Retail Stores

### 1. Rockbot
Rockbot is a streaming media platform for businesses offering licensed background music, digital signage, TV programming, audio messaging, and retail media advertising through one unified platform. Founded in 2009 and backed by Google, Rockbot serves nearly 50,000 businesses across North America.
- **Key Strength:** Single-platform solution for music, TV, signage, and advertising. Backed by Google. Interactive Rockbot Request feature lets guests request songs.
- **Music Library:** 18M+ songs

### 2. Stingray
Stingray is a Canadian public company (TSX: RAY.A/RAY.B) providing commercial music, digital signage, in-store audio advertising, and AI-driven consumer insights. Stingray Advertising is North America's largest retail audio advertising network, reaching 928M+ shopping visits monthly across 25,100+ locations.
- **Key Strength:** North America's largest retail audio advertising network with 25,100+ locations and 928M+ monthly shopping visits. Publicly traded with ~1,000 employees globally.

### 3. MTI
MTI is an in-store media provider offering background music, overhead messaging, and digital signage solutions for businesses. The company focuses on helping brands create consistent audio experiences across multiple locations with curated music programming and targeted messaging.
- **Key Strength:** Personalized service with direct account management and custom music programming for multi-location businesses

### 4. Mood Media
Mood Media is the world's leading in-store media provider, offering background music, digital signage, scent marketing, AV systems, and overhead messaging. Formerly Muzak, the company serves over 100,000 businesses globally with a comprehensive suite of customer experience solutions.
- **Key Strength:** Largest global in-store media provider with 88+ years of industry heritage (Muzak legacy) and 100+ expert music designers worldwide
- **Music Library:** 120M+ tracks

### 5. Soundtrack Your Brand
Soundtrack Your Brand is a Spotify-backed commercial music streaming platform that provides fully licensed background music for businesses. Known for strong UX and the largest commercially licensed music catalog, it offers on-demand track selection, custom playlist building, and multi-location management.
- **Key Strength:** Spotify-backed with the largest commercially licensed catalog. Only major platform offering true on-demand song selection and Spotify playlist import.
- **Music Library:** 58M+ songs

### 6. QSIC
QSIC is an AI-powered in-store audio platform that helps retailers monetize and measure in-store audio as a retail media channel. Founded in Australia in 2012, QSIC powers 7-Eleven's Gulp Radio across 12,000+ stores and reaches 100M+ shoppers monthly. Raised $25M Series B in January 2025 led by Hedosophia.
- **Key Strength:** AI-powered audio platform with patented ambient noise technology, closed-loop sales attribution, and AI-generated ad creative (Lucy). Powers 7-Eleven Gulp Radio across 12,000+ stores.

## What to Look For

- Content filtering and appropriateness for retail stores
- Multi-location management dashboard
- Commercial music licensing included
- Hardware compatibility with existing systems
- Reliable uptime and support
- Scalable pricing as you grow

## Pricing for Retail Stores

Budget: $15-25/mo per location. Mid-range: $25-75/mo. Enterprise: custom pricing. Factor in hardware, installation, and any required AV equipment.

h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Florida
intro: Playing music in your business in Florida? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Florida. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Florida may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Florida need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Florida

All businesses in Florida that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Florida

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Florida

Businesses in Florida caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Florida.

## Florida Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Florida, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.

title: How retail media network advertiser onboarding works
meta_title: How Retail Media Network Advertiser Onboarding Works | InStoreIndex

h1: How Does Retail Media Network Advertiser Onboarding Work?
intro: Retail media network advertiser onboarding typically involves account setup, creative asset submission, audience targeting configuration, and campaign launch. Most networks require advertisers to complete a registration process, agree to content guidelines, upload approved creative assets, and select targeting parameters before campaigns go live. The process takes anywhere from a few days on self-serve platforms to several weeks for managed-service campaigns with custom integrations.
body_content:
## Steps in the Advertiser Onboarding Process

### 1. Account Registration and Approval
Advertisers apply through the retail media network's portal. Networks verify the brand is sold in their stores and meets advertising guidelines. Some networks restrict categories like tobacco, alcohol, or competing private-label products.

### 2. Creative Asset Submission
Advertisers provide creative assets matching the network's specifications. For in-store audio, this typically means 15- or 30-second audio spots. For digital screens, it means static images or video files at specific resolutions. Most networks review and approve creative before it goes live.

### 3. Audience and Store Targeting
Advertisers select which stores, regions, or audience segments to target. Advanced networks offer targeting based on purchase history, loyalty data, time of day, and demographic profiles. Simpler networks offer store-level or regional targeting.

### 4. Campaign Configuration
Setting flight dates, budget caps, frequency caps, and daypart scheduling. Managed-service campaigns may include a strategy session with the network's sales team to optimize placement and timing.

### 5. Measurement Setup
Connecting first-party sales data for closed-loop attribution. This often requires data-sharing agreements and technical integration with POS systems or loyalty platforms.

## Common Onboarding Challenges

The biggest friction points are creative approval timelines, data integration complexity, and inconsistent specifications across different retail media networks. Brands advertising across multiple retailers often struggle with fragmented workflows and varying technical requirements.

title: Music Licensing Requirements in Delaware (2026)
meta_title: Music Licensing for Business in Delaware (2026)
meta_description: Music licensing requirements for businesses in Delaware. Understand PRO licenses, penalties, and compliance options for 2026.
h1: Music Licensing Requirements for Businesses in Delaware
intro: Playing music in your business in Delaware? You need to understand the music licensing requirements that apply to commercial establishments in Delaware. Federal copyright law requires businesses to obtain public performance licenses, and Delaware may have additional state-specific regulations. Here's what businesses in Delaware need to know about music licensing in 2026.
body_content:
## Music Licensing Requirements in Delaware

All businesses in Delaware that play music publicly must comply with federal copyright law, which requires public performance licenses from performing rights organizations (PROs).

## Required Licenses

- **ASCAP:** Covers ~900,000 songwriters and 18M+ works
- **BMI:** Covers 1.4M+ songwriters and 22.4M+ works
- **SESAC:** Invitation-only, covers ~30,000 affiliates
- **GMR:** Newer PRO covering additional works

## How to Comply in Delaware

The easiest way to ensure compliance is to use a licensed commercial music service like Mood Media, Rockbot, Soundtrack Your Brand, or Cloud Cover Music. These services include all necessary PRO licenses in their subscription, so you don't need to negotiate separately with each organization.

## Penalties for Non-Compliance in Delaware

Businesses in Delaware caught playing unlicensed music face statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song, with willful infringement penalties up to $150,000 per song. PROs actively audit businesses and have filed lawsuits against establishments across Delaware.

## Delaware Music Providers

All major commercial music providers serve businesses in Delaware, including Mood Media, Rockbot, Stingray, Soundtrack Your Brand, Cloud Cover Music, and others.
